'''Larry D. Nichols''' (born December 27, 1939) is an American puzzle designer. He grew up in [[Xenia, Ohio|Xenia]], [[Ohio]], and studied chemistry at [[DePauw University]] in  [[Greencastle, Indiana]], before moving to Massachusetts to attend Harvard Graduate School. He is best known for the invention of [[mechanical puzzle]]s such as "The Nichols Cube Puzzle" (1972), patent US3655201.

==The Nichols Cube Puzzle (Twizzle)==

In 1957, 17 years before  [[Ernő Rubik|Dr. Rubik's]] invention popularly known as the “[[Rubik's Cube]]”, Dr. Nichols conceived of a twist cube puzzle with six colored faces. It was a 2×2×2 cube assembled from eight unit cubes with magnets on their inside faces, allowing the cubes to rotate in groups of four around three axes. The object of the puzzle was to mix the colors on the faces of the cube and then restore them.

After making many preliminary models, in 1968 a working prototype was constructed, and on April 11, 1972, U.S. patent 3,655,201 was issued covering the Nichols' Cube. The patent focused on the 2×2×2 puzzle but mentioned the possibility of larger versions.<ref name="sp">{{Cite patent|number=US3655201A|title=Pattern forming puzzle and method with pieces rotatable in groups|gdate=1972-04-11|invent1=Nichols|inventor1-first=Larry D.|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US3655201/en}}</ref>

Nichols' patents became the subject of a court hearing between his employer and the Ideal Toy Company.<ref name="sp3">[http://blog.jipel.law.nyu.edu/2015/10/the-legal-puzzle-of-the-rubiks-cube/ The Legal Puzzle of the Rubik’s Cube]</ref><ref name="sp4">[https://www.nytimes.com/1984/12/03/business/cube-is-a-problem-to-cbs.html NY Times: Cube Is A Problem To CBS]</ref><ref name="sp5">[http://www.firstversions.com/2015/08/rubiks-cube.html First Version]</ref> In 1985, a U.S. District Court ruled that Rubik's Cube infringed the Nichols patent, but in 1986 the Court of Appeals ruled that only the smaller 2×2×2 Rubik's Pocket Cube was guilty of infringement, and not the popular 3×3×3 Rubik's Cube.<ref name="sp1">[http://www.ageofpuzzles.com/Masters/LarryDNichols/LarryDNichols.htm Age of Puzzles]</ref>

=== Analogues of the invention ===
* Manipulative toy William O Gustafson 1960 <ref name = "sp10">[https://patents.google.com/patent/US3081089 Patent US3081089: 'Manipulatable toy' by William O Gustafson 1960]</ref>
* [[Rubik's Cube]] 1974 <ref name = "sp11">[https://patents.google.com/patent/US4378117 Patent US4378117: 'Spatial intelligent toy' by Erno Rubik 1974]</ref>
* Frank Fox got a British patent for a spherical sliding puzzle in 1974 <ref name = "spq1">[https://www.jaapsch.net/puzzles/patents/gb1344259.pdf Patent GB1344259: 'Amusement device' by  Frank Fox 1974]</ref>
* Terutoshi Ishige received a Japanese patent for a 3x3x3 in 1976 <ref name = "spw">{{cite magazine |last1=Kim |first1=Mark H. |last2=Molteni |first2=Megan |last3=Allain |first3=Rhett |last4=Simon |first4=Matt |last5=Stockton |first5=Nick |title=Jan. 30, 1975: Rubik Applies for Patent on Magic Cube |date=January 30, 2009 |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2009/01/dayintech-0130/}}</ref>

==Career==

Nichols received a degree in chemistry in 1958 from DePauw University, where he was a Rector Scholar, and went on to earn a doctorate at Harvard. As a Harvard student, he invented and produced games and puzzles. He became chief scientist for the Moleculon Research Corporation of Cambridge, Massachusetts, and invented one of its  primary products, Poroplastic, in 1973. Poroplastic film has the mechanical properties of a typical plastic, but is able to hold large quantities of almost any liquid within tiny pores. Usage of Poroplastic materials centers on controlled drug delivery and environmental health and safety products.<ref name="sp2">[http://www.depauw.edu/news-media/latest-news/details/31162/ Role of Larry Nichols '58 in Inventing Famous Toy is Recalled]</ref>

== Personal Life ==
He has lived with his wife Karen in Arlington, Massachusetts since 1959.

==See also==
[[Arthur S. Obermayer]] was the founder-owner of Moleculon Research Corporation where Nichols was Chief Scientist. Obermayer encouraged and helped to patent the Nichols Cube.
